newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices slip back, soybeans power higher.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices slip back, soybeans power higher.

text.p: Coffee prices suffered a setback Thursday following their recent rapid advance but soybeans powered to the highest level in 5-1/2 months.
Coffee prices spiraled sharply lower toward the end of the day on profit-taking one day after the market surged to its highest level in nearly 2-1/2 years.
Traders said the sell-off was all but inevitable following the market's stunning rise.
Coffee prices, which have gained more than 50 percent since the start of the year, had climbed more than 15 percent in the last week alone before selling off Thursday.
"No matter how bullish the funds are, at times profit-taking sets in and you have a correction," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "The market just needed to take a breather."

Talk that Colombia would open registrations -- a formality required before private exporters can sell their coffee on the world market -- for April-June coffee shipments may have exacerbated the slide, dealers said.
After the close of trading, Colombian coffee officials confirmed April-June registrations for private exporters would be opened on Friday.
May coffee futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange closed off 6.95 cents per pound at 193.70 cents.
Soybean futures closed sharply higher boosted by strong U.S. export sales and reports a leading analytical firm had cut its estimate for U.S. ending stocks for the 1996/97 year ending Aug. 31.
The Agriculture Department on Thursday said 456,100 metric tons of U.S. soybeans were sold for export in the week ended Feb. 27, above trade expectations for 300,000 to 400,000 tons.

Trade sources also said Sparks Companies cut their 1996-97 ending stocks projection to 130 million bushels, below the Agriculture Department's February estimate of 140 million bushels. The Memphis, Tenn.-based analytical firm declined to comment on the rumour.
News that strike talks at Brazil's Paranagua port had been delayed provided a further supportive factor. Dock workers went on strike Wednesday following a pay dispute.
Traders said commodity funds were major buyers, purchasing at least 25 million bushels and some pegged the total as high as 40 million bushels.
March futures on the Chicago Board of Trade closed 16-3/4 cents a bushel up at $8.18, just below an earlier 5-1/2 month high for the nearby contract of $8.18-1/2.
In New York, heating oil futures shook off their end-of-the-winter blues and settled with sharp gains as technical strength sparked a round of short covering.

"Heating oil has fallen so much. Part of the rise today was technical, but there are a lot of shorts in crude and heating oil, and that led to covering," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.

"Refined products are what the led the market," Saucer added. On the New York Mercantile Exchange, April heating oil ended up 0.89 cent at 53.43 cents a gallon. April gasoline ended up 1.15 cents a gallon at 64.48 cents.
April crude oil finished 45 cents higher at $20.94 a barrel. Traders bid up gasoline before the start of spring, when gasoline typically rallies ahead of the summer driving season.
